title: Distributed Systems — Autonomous AI Organizations
footer: Source-backed component evidence and founder-reported business facts. Architecture animations are explanatory, not live telemetry.

scenes.title: Autonomous AI organizations
scenes.notes: Thank you for taking the time. Distributed Systems is building infrastructure for autonomous AI organizations. Our claim is not that general intelligence is solved; our claim is that useful AI needs an operating layer around it: authority, tools, memory, records, and recovery. We have built the substrate, we have been paid to apply it, and we are now raising to make it repeatable.
scenes.source: Founder vision, October 30 2026. Autonomous organizations are the company's goal, not a claim of achieved general intelligence. Product source: https://distributed.systems/ .
scenes.cue: The reason we start with the organization—not the model—is that intelligence by itself does not carry responsibility.

text.text: Building the next generation of superintelligence

scenes.deliveryCue: Start with the company in one breath. Do not lead with the architecture yet.

scenes.title: AI needs an organization around it
scenes.notes: A model can produce a brilliant answer and still fail as a business. A business needs ownership, permissions, persistent state, handoffs, and a record of what happened. Our thesis is that AI needs an organization around it: a durable structure that tells the system what it may do, what must be recorded, and who accepts the result.
scenes.source: Investment thesis, based on founder YC pitch https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YUNJ2eLQWhw 01:38-02:31 and current product architecture. Company strategy, not a measured market-wide finding.
scenes.cue: Our answer is a shared stack that turns that thesis into an executable system.
scenes.deliveryCue: Make the gap concrete in business terms: responsibility, persistence, and accountability.
scenes.subtitle: The operating layer that turns intelligent work into an accountable organization.

scenes.title: One stack for work and organizations
scenes.notes: This is the architecture we are building. DSCO is the local-first harness for executing work. Tool Management exposes capabilities and their schemas. Router and Chimera dispatch work across models and providers. GraphSub gives the system connected state and persistence. HEAT is the first application-shaped proof point. These components are real and inspectable, while the depth of their integration is still a diligence question.

scenes.title: DSCO puts the stack to work
scenes.notes: DSCO turns a mandate into work. It decomposes the objective, delegates bounded tasks, executes through approved tools, verifies the result, and records what happened. If a premise changes or a step fails, the run can recover instead of silently disappearing. That is the difference between asking a model for an answer and operating a system that can be accountable for work.
scenes.source: DSCO product description: https://distributed.systems/ . Founder explicitly identifies dsco-cli as harness for executing work and automating business actions. Diagram is conceptual product workflow, not a UI screenshot or claim every integration is production-tested.
scenes.cue: The design boundary that matters most is the separation between a model’s judgment and the authority to act.

text.text: Work becomes an accountable execution loop

scenes.deliveryCue: Explain the loop as a workflow, not as a feature list.

scenes.title: Authority is separate from model judgment
scenes.notes: The model’s confidence is not authority. Authority comes from the mandate, the capability boundary, the budget, the stop conditions, and the escalation path. DSCO’s governed execution and Chronicle receipts are the implementation evidence behind this design. We are not asking an investor to take a security guarantee on faith; we are showing the control surface we have built and the proof still required.
scenes.source: DSCO source and implementation evidence: https://github.com/arthurcolle/dsco
scenes.cue: Once authority is explicit, capabilities can be shared without making the whole system opaque.

scenes.title: A shared action layer across services
scenes.notes: Tool Management is the shared action surface. It discovers capabilities, exposes schemas, executes calls, composes workflows, and keeps external effects behind explicit boundaries. That lets us add capabilities without giving every model a new private integration. The important product property is not a large tool count; it is that the authority and result shape remain legible as the system grows.
scenes.cue: The action layer becomes much more useful when routing and memory are first-class parts of the same system.

scenes.title: Intelligence and organizational memory
scenes.notes: The stack needs two more things: intelligence can be routed to the right model or provider, and organizational memory can persist beyond a single context window. Router and Chimera handle bounded dispatch and metering. GraphSub provides connected state, persistence, and query primitives. This is component evidence, not a claim of production scale; the value is that the pieces have a common operating contract.
scenes.cue: HEAT is where we are applying this architecture to a concrete operating problem.

scenes.title: HEAT is our first organization-shaped application
scenes.notes: HEAT Trading is our first organization-shaped application and the first spin-out business. It combines research systems with ingestion, tools, realtime interfaces, and operating workflows. The public product is a research preview; order-placement schedules are paused. So this is not a profitability, returns, or unattended-live-trading claim. It is our first concrete environment for proving the organization layer against a demanding workflow.
scenes.source: Sources: dsco-heat-trading/docs/CURRENT_RUNTIME.md, checkout81c8b62 Oct17 modified locally, reviewed Oct30. Hetzner/Neon path, ingestion, authenticated MCP, realtime API, Temporal. No profitability, fund regulation, completed legal entity or live unattended execution claim.
scenes.cue: The larger opportunity is not a single agent; it is an organization that persists when agents change.

text.text: A proving ground for organization-shaped work

scenes.title: Organizations persist beyond a single agent
scenes.notes: An organization should not disappear when one agent stops, a provider changes, or a founder hands off a task. Our Organization Compiler work is aimed at projecting a durable organization across runtime, router, graph, and agent surfaces. The prototype direction is real, but production admission is incomplete. The investment opportunity is to turn that architecture into an independently operating system, not to pretend that milestone is already finished.
scenes.source: Product direction grounded in Organization Compiler SYSTEM-STATUS.md, Aug20 artifacts: deterministic OrganizationSpec to EntityCapsule projections across runtime/router/graph/durable agents. Production admission incomplete. This slide describes target architecture and prototype capability, not completed independent business operation.

scenes.title: A shared-stack business model
scenes.notes: The business model starts with scoped paid engagements. We enter through a workflow where the customer can define acceptance, permissions, and value. We then turn the repeated parts into operating infrastructure and, where there is a strong wedge, into a focused application or spin-out. The company website already offers six-month project engagements; future recurring economics are a plan, not contracted ARR.
scenes.source: Founder YC pitch https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YUNJ2eLQWhw 00:57-01:11 and 02:01-02:31. Website offers scoped six-month project engagements. Future application/spinout economics are strategy, not contracted recurring revenue or completed spinouts.
scenes.cue: We are early, so the traction claim is deliberately narrow and easy to audit.

scenes.title: Target customers and deployment strategy
scenes.notes: Our initial customers are teams with expensive workflows that cross systems and require a clear record of who did what. We start with a bounded process, define acceptance, and earn the right to expand. Defense and intelligence are target markets because deployment ownership and controlled execution matter there, but we are not claiming a defense contract, accreditation, or existing pipeline.
scenes.source: Proposed go-to-market based on founder direction, not a claim of existing pipeline, government customers, certification or procurement access. Commercial approach: scoped paid engagements, consistent with https://distributed.systems/ .
scenes.cue: To support that strategy, we want to own the capacity the stack depends on.

scenes.title: Owned compute supports the shared stack
scenes.notes: The compute strategy is not a claim that we already have a large GPU fleet. We have evidence of owned workers completing dated deterministic CPU jobs. The proposed $6 million raise allocates roughly 80 percent—$4.8 million—to physical compute we intend to purchase and operate at Montrose Data Center, 401 Nina Place, Rockville, Maryland. The facility, power, cooling, network, equipment, and purchase terms still need diligence; we will release spend against measured workloads and utilization gates.

scenes.title: Founder-led execution
scenes.notes: This is founder-led execution. I have built the systems, sold the work, and operated the early infrastructure, but that is not the same as a finished company. The repository review confirms that the named components exist; it does not prove sole authorship of every line, audited performance, or founder-independent delivery. The raise is partly about converting personal execution into a team, process, and product that can stand on its own.

scenes.title: Raising $6m to build autonomous organizations
scenes.notes: We are raising $6 million. Roughly 80 percent, or $4.8 million, is planned for owned physical compute; the remaining $1.2 million is an implied planning bucket for product, delivery, evidence, people, and operating reserve. This is a proposed use of funds, not a costed budget, a valuation, or money already committed. The milestones are repeat paid deployments, measured operating economics, completed production admission, and an organization that can operate beyond the founder.

scenes.title: Evidence and current readiness
scenes.notes: Let me close with the honest status. DSCO has governed tool execution and Chronicle receipts. Tool Management has discovery, schemas, execution, and workflows. Router and Chimera have dispatch and metering. GraphSub has graph, query, and persistence primitives. HEAT has ingestion, tools, realtime interfaces, and workflows. This is component evidence from an October 30 read-only review, not a fresh end-to-end production test: HEAT order placement is paused, organization-compiler production admission is incomplete, services revenue is not ARR, and Mainline is still in process. The raise is to turn these components into a repeatable, independently accepted business.
